question.problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ if 

$$
{y}^{′}+2y=5{u}_{3}(t)\cdot {e}^{2t-6}\,,\,y(0)=5,
$$

where ${u}_{3}(t)=u(t-3)$ is the unit step function.

$Y(s)=\frac{5}{s+2}\,+\,$
{{field-1}},$\,s>2$
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{′}+2y\} & =L\{5{u}_{3}(t)\cdot {e}^{2t-6}\} \\ L\{{y}^{′}\}+2L\{y\} & =L\{5{u}_{3}(t)\cdot {e}^{2t-6}\}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L\{{y}^{′}\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=5:$

$$
L\{{y}^{′}\}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)-5
$$

To find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term 

$$
5{u}_{3}(t)\cdot {e}^{2t-6}
$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=3$ and $f(t)=5{e}^{2t-6}.$

Now, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states

$$
L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)\}={e}^{-as}\cdot L\{f(t+a)\}.
$$

  

So, by the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{5u(t-3)\cdot {e}^{2t-6}\} & ={e}^{-3s}\cdot L\{5{e}^{2(t+3)-6}\} \\  & ={e}^{-3s}\cdot L\{5{e}^{2t}\} \\  & ={e}^{-3s}\cdot \frac{5}{s-2} \\  & =\frac{5{e}^{-3s}}{s-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute these back into our transformed differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{′}\}+2L\{y\} & =L\{5{u}_{3}(t){e}^{2t-6}\} \\ (sY(s)-5)+2Y(s) & =\frac{5{e}^{-3s}}{s-2} \\ (s+2)Y(s)-5 & =\frac{5{e}^{-3s}}{s-2} \\ (s+2)Y(s) & =5+\frac{5{e}^{-3s}}{s-2} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{5}{s+2}+\frac{5{e}^{-3s}}{(s-2)(s+2)}\end{aligned}
$$
